title: Deployment infrastructure becomes part of the product
lead: Suppliers are building not only robots but also test sites, service teams and commercial-scaling structures. For buyers, maturity depends on integration cost, support, acceptance conditions and measured results at the operating site.

news.title: Hido II enters limited deployment for automated indoor mapping
news.summary: Hidonix has launched a limited deployment program for the Hido II rover to collect spatial data inside buildings. Under technician supervision, it follows predefined routes, avoids obstacles, climbs stairs and positions an acquisition module with a robotic arm.
news.details: Hidonix Industries announced the launch of Hido II on November 18 as a mobile rover for mapping complex indoor spaces. After showing a prototype at CES 2026, the company is selecting US venues for a limited early-access program. A technician remains on site and supervises operation, so the release describes controlled deployment rather than a fully independent surveying service.
news.technical_novelty: The rover follows predefined routes, detects obstacles and replans its path. A rocker-bogie suspension is intended for uneven ground and conventional stairs; the platform can rotate in place and move laterally. A robotic arm repeatedly positions the geomagnetic acquisition module, while a 2K stereo camera and Ouster lidar provide depth reconstruction, obstacle awareness and a 360-degree point cloud. Stated runtime is about five to eight hours depending on activity.
news.engineering_impact: A venue operator needs more than survey speed: crew travel, route preparation, closed walkways and repeat surveys after a building change all affect cost. The limited program discloses no price, fleet availability or service terms. Economics can be assessed only after comparing mapped area per shift, technician labor and the navigation quality produced from the collected data.
news.limitations: In a comparative test, the company reports a 50% reduction in mapping time and positioning error up to five times lower than manual collection with the ION App. It does not publish the method, venue count, route area or error distribution. The figures are therefore supplier-reported internal results, not an independent evaluation of a production fleet.
news.evidence_status: Official organization announcement; reported results and plans remain source claims rather than independent operational verification.
news.body:
Hidonix Industries announced the launch of Hido II on November 18 as a mobile rover for mapping complex indoor spaces. After showing a prototype at CES 2026, the company is selecting US venues for a limited early-access program. A technician remains on site and supervises operation, so the release describes controlled deployment rather than a fully independent surveying service.

The rover follows predefined routes, detects obstacles and replans its path. A rocker-bogie suspension is intended for uneven ground and conventional stairs; the platform can rotate in place and move laterally. A robotic arm repeatedly positions the geomagnetic acquisition module, while a 2K stereo camera and Ouster lidar provide depth reconstruction, obstacle awareness and a 360-degree point cloud. Stated runtime is about five to eight hours depending on activity.

A venue operator needs more than survey speed: crew travel, route preparation, closed walkways and repeat surveys after a building change all affect cost. The limited program discloses no price, fleet availability or service terms. Economics can be assessed only after comparing mapped area per shift, technician labor and the navigation quality produced from the collected data.

In a comparative test, the company reports a 50% reduction in mapping time and positioning error up to five times lower than manual collection with the ION App. It does not publish the method, venue count, route area or error distribution. The figures are therefore supplier-reported internal results, not an independent evaluation of a production fleet.

news.title: Agility Robotics reshapes leadership after becoming a public company
news.summary: Agility Robotics appointed a president, chief product officer and chief administrative officer after its November Nasdaq listing. It links the structure to scaling Digit 5 sales and deployments, while the cited $300 million represents potential order value subject to contractual milestones.
news.details: Agility Robotics announced three appointments on November 18 after completing its combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI and listing on Nasdaq on November 4. Daniel Diez became president responsible for the commercial business. Christopher Sullivan became chief product officer while retaining a connection to customer success. Ana Lang became chief administrative officer and continues to oversee legal, people, governance and risk functions.
news.technical_novelty: The company frames the change as preparation to move from individual programs toward larger Digit deployments. Diez leads sales and partnerships, Sullivan connects product strategy and execution with customer-site experience, and Lang builds public-company processes. Agility cites more than 65,000 hours of real-world robot operation and over $300 million in committed multi-year Digit 5 orders, but the latter is potential value subject to contractual milestones and product specifications.
news.engineering_impact: Separating sales, product and corporate-control responsibility is a public-company move toward scale. Customers need to see whether it produces predictable delivery, support and contract terms. The potential $300 million cannot be treated as recognized revenue because fulfillment depends on contractual stages and product specifications.
news.limitations: The release announces no new contract, robot delivery, production capacity or reliability result. The appointments show which functions Agility is strengthening: commercial scale, product-to-deployment feedback and corporate control. Future deployments and order value remain company expectations exposed to manufacturing, technical and market risks.
news.evidence_status: Official organization announcement; reported results and plans remain source claims rather than independent operational verification.
news.body:
Agility Robotics announced three appointments on November 18 after completing its combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI and listing on Nasdaq on November 4. Daniel Diez became president responsible for the commercial business. Christopher Sullivan became chief product officer while retaining a connection to customer success. Ana Lang became chief administrative officer and continues to oversee legal, people, governance and risk functions.

The company frames the change as preparation to move from individual programs toward larger Digit deployments. Diez leads sales and partnerships, Sullivan connects product strategy and execution with customer-site experience, and Lang builds public-company processes. Agility cites more than 65,000 hours of real-world robot operation and over $300 million in committed multi-year Digit 5 orders, but the latter is potential value subject to contractual milestones and product specifications.

Separating sales, product and corporate-control responsibility is a public-company move toward scale. Customers need to see whether it produces predictable delivery, support and contract terms. The potential $300 million cannot be treated as recognized revenue because fulfillment depends on contractual stages and product specifications.

The release announces no new contract, robot delivery, production capacity or reliability result. news.title: SCHUNK spin-off TACTILIA takes modular robot hand toward industrial market
news.summary: SCHUNK Humanoid Robotics, founded in January, now operates as TACTILIA Robotics. It is developing a modular hand for humanoids, cobots and mobile manipulators, supported by testing access to 15 SCHUNK CoLabs.
news.details: SCHUNK announced on November 18 that its January spin-off SCHUNK Humanoid Robotics now operates as TACTILIA Robotics. The independent Munich company is developing a modular robotic hand for production and logistics tasks. Markus Netzer leads the business, while the parent group supplies gripping expertise, test infrastructure and access to industrial customers.
news.technical_novelty: The developers aim to combine mechanics, sensors, actuators, software and physical-AI methods in one platform. The hand is intended for humanoids, collaborative robots and mobile manipulators rather than one robot body. Customer testing is planned through 15 SCHUNK CoLabs, where specific operations can be evaluated and adapted before deployment.
news.engineering_impact: The spin-off combines a focused team with access to SCHUNK's 15 application centers, but commercial terms are absent. Buyers need price, lead time, warranty, grip-skill training and responsibility for manipulator integration. The test network can reduce task-selection risk, yet it does not establish product lifetime.
news.limitations: The release gives no finger count for the new platform, degrees of freedom, force, accuracy, cycle life, interfaces, price or delivery date. Language about bringing a product to market states the company's direction, not a confirmed production shipment. Verified facts are the new name, independent structure, location and stated development and validation program.
news.evidence_status: Official organization announcement; reported results and plans remain source claims rather than independent operational verification.
news.body:
SCHUNK announced on November 18 that its January spin-off SCHUNK Humanoid Robotics now operates as TACTILIA Robotics. The independent Munich company is developing a modular robotic hand for production and logistics tasks. Markus Netzer leads the business, while the parent group supplies gripping expertise, test infrastructure and access to industrial customers.

The developers aim to combine mechanics, sensors, actuators, software and physical-AI methods in one platform. The hand is intended for humanoids, collaborative robots and mobile manipulators rather than one robot body. Customer testing is planned through 15 SCHUNK CoLabs, where specific operations can be evaluated and adapted before deployment.

The spin-off combines a focused team with access to SCHUNK's 15 application centers, but commercial terms are absent. Buyers need price, lead time, warranty, grip-skill training and responsibility for manipulator integration. The test network can reduce task-selection risk, yet it does not establish product lifetime. A separate test should change objects without manual reprogramming: how many examples the hand needs, how grasp time changes and whether force remains stable as actuators warm. Those records would show whether modularity is a product property rather than only an organizational goal.

The release gives no finger count for the new platform, degrees of freedom, force, accuracy, cycle life, interfaces, price or delivery date. Language about bringing a product to market states the company's direction, not a confirmed production shipment. Verified facts are the new name, independent structure, location and stated development and validation program.

news.title: Tokyo lab opens to demonstrate and test robots before deployment
news.summary: ImageONE and Big Hands have opened IMO Robotics LAB in Tokyo to demonstrate robots and test possible use cases. Galbot G1 is the first displayed machine, while medical-facility work is the stated initial focus for future proofs of concept.
news.details: ImageONE announced the opening of IMO Robotics LAB at its Osaki, Tokyo headquarters on November 18. It created the site with Big Hands, which provides robot products, specialist engineers and technical information. ImageONE supplies the facility and coordinates operations, marketing and contact with prospective customers.
news.technical_novelty: The lab has begun displaying the mobile, dual-arm Galbot G1. Its operators plan to add humanoids from other manufacturers, bionic devices, quadrupeds and robotic hands. Beyond demonstrations, the site is intended for proofs of concept, deployment proposals, engineer training and seminars, with medical-facility work named as the first area of attention.
news.engineering_impact: A local demonstration site can lower the cost of first evaluation but cannot replace a customer-site test. A proof of concept needs a process owner, integration budget, supplier responsibilities, data protection and support plan. The commercial signal will be a named paid project with a measured result.
news.limitations: The company confirms the opening and the physical G1 display. It names no medical process, customer, test date, success criterion or paid project. The lab therefore creates a place for task selection and integration work, but it does not yet show that the displayed robot performs regular hospital duties.
news.evidence_status: Official organization announcement; reported results and plans remain source claims rather than independent operational verification.
news.body:
ImageONE announced the opening of IMO Robotics LAB at its Osaki, Tokyo headquarters on November 18. It created the site with Big Hands, which provides robot products, specialist engineers and technical information. ImageONE supplies the facility and coordinates operations, marketing and contact with prospective customers.

The lab has begun displaying the mobile, dual-arm Galbot G1. Its operators plan to add humanoids from other manufacturers, bionic devices, quadrupeds and robotic hands. Beyond demonstrations, the site is intended for proofs of concept, deployment proposals, engineer training and seminars, with medical-facility work named as the first area of attention.

A local demonstration site can lower the cost of first evaluation but cannot replace a customer-site test. A proof of concept needs a process owner, integration budget, supplier responsibilities, data protection and support plan. The commercial signal will be a named paid project with a measured result. Each proof of concept should end with a protocol rather than a demonstration: attempt count, success share, interventions, stops and site modifications. A later customer could then distinguish what is repeatable from what depended on a prepared scene and supplier specialists.

The company confirms the opening and the physical G1 display. It names no medical process, customer, test date, success criterion or paid project. The lab therefore creates a place for task selection and integration work, but it does not yet show that the displayed robot performs regular hospital duties.

news.title: GlobalFoundries expands Spot fleet and prepares first chip-fab trials for Atlas
news.summary: GlobalFoundries will expand Spot quadruped deployments across semiconductor sites in the United States, Germany and Singapore. It also plans to begin Atlas humanoid trials in early 2027, although no specific Atlas task has been named.
news.details: Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries announced an expanded semiconductor-fab robotics program on November 17. Spot will perform automated rounds and collect equipment data at sites in New York, Vermont, Dresden and Singapore. GlobalFoundries will also become the first Atlas customer outside the automotive industry, but onsite humanoid testing is scheduled only for early 2027.
news.technical_novelty: Two Spots in Singapore have traveled nearly 900 kilometers and completed more than 90,000 inspections in sub-fab areas since April, according to the companies, with a 99% mission success rate. After hardware and software updates, 875 routine inspections were redeployed in two weeks, and GlobalFoundries plans to more than double that number. The release does not define mission success or disclose interventions and downtime.
news.engineering_impact: Spot expansion follows four years with the customer and a measured volume of rounds, making it more mature than the future Atlas pilot. Economics depend on avoided downtime, support cost and the share of inspections that need no repeat visit by a person. The humanoid first needs a task where flexibility justifies integration effort and early-product risk.
news.limitations: The Atlas program starts with a skills-development workshop to identify use cases, assess site readiness and integration needs, and begin training for specific actions. That is not yet humanoid production work or an order for a stated robot count. The confirmed operating deployment concerns Spot; Atlas remains a planned trial with tasks still to be selected.
news.evidence_status: Official organization announcement; reported results and plans remain source claims rather than independent operational verification.
news.body:
Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries announced an expanded semiconductor-fab robotics program on November 17. Spot will perform automated rounds and collect equipment data at sites in New York, Vermont, Dresden and Singapore. GlobalFoundries will also become the first Atlas customer outside the automotive industry, but onsite humanoid testing is scheduled only for early 2027.

Two Spots in Singapore have traveled nearly 900 kilometers and completed more than 90,000 inspections in sub-fab areas since April, according to the companies, with a 99% mission success rate. After hardware and software updates, 875 routine inspections were redeployed in two weeks, and GlobalFoundries plans to more than double that number. The release does not define mission success or disclose interventions and downtime.

Spot expansion follows four years with the customer and a measured volume of rounds, making it more mature than the future Atlas pilot. Economics depend on avoided downtime, support cost and the share of inspections that need no repeat visit by a person. The humanoid first needs a task where flexibility justifies integration effort and early-product risk.

The Atlas program starts with a skills-development workshop to identify use cases, assess site readiness and integration needs, and begin training for specific actions. That is not yet humanoid production work or an order for a stated robot count. The confirmed operating deployment concerns Spot; Atlas remains a planned trial with tasks still to be selected.
